idiom_name: renders_one / renders_many declare the family; the parent component owns the state in Ruby
implementation_notes: In Rails the pattern arrives through ViewComponent's slot API: the parent declares renders_one :option or renders_many :options, the call site supplies cooperating sub-components, and the parent decides in its template where they render - the guide presents slots as the way to render multiple blocks of content, including other components. What replaces the JSX family is ordinary Ruby composition: the parent component owns the state in its instance variables, passes it into the sub-component instances it builds, and enforces invariants in Ruby, while the template only places the slots. Because the children are real objects with references to the parent, the pattern needs no implicit channel at all - which also removes its main failure mode.
code_sketch:
class SelectComponent < ViewComponent::Base
  renders_many :options, "SelectOptionComponent"    # children declare themselves

  def initialize(selected: nil)
    @selected = selected                            # parent owns the state
  end

  def option(value:, label:)                        # factory for the call site
    SelectOptionComponent.new(value:, label:, selected: value == @selected)
  end
end
# template: <%= render options %> - the parent decides rendering and order
pitfalls: Slots render where the parent's template says, not where the call site wrote them: a declared slot that is never rendered disappears silently.
Reusing one component instance across slots shares its state; components are cheap, build a new one per slot instead of memoizing.
Calling the slot before the component's state is set (a before_render expectation) yields children with stale values - compute the state in the constructor or in before_render.

variants.name: Rails content_for/capture: children register blocks, the layout yields them
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-ViewComponent form is Rails' capture/content_for: a child template registers a named block with content_for(:name) and the parent layout renders it with yield :name, which is exactly the implicit registration shape - children declare themselves, the parent decides position and presence. It has no component object, so there is nowhere to enforce an invariant in Ruby: the shared state lives in controller instance variables, which makes this the manual realization of the family. Use it for page-level composition (sidebar, head, footer), and move to components when the family needs its own state or its children must be individually configured.
variants.idiom_name: content_for(name) in child templates + yield :name in the parent layout
variants.code_sketch:
<%# child view: register implicitly %>
<% content_for :sidebar do %><nav>...</nav><% end %>
<%# parent layout: decide order and presence %>
<body><aside><%= yield :sidebar %></aside><%= yield %></body>
pitfalls: content_for blocks append in capture order, so defining the same name twice concatenates rather than replaces unless the capture is flushed.
Nothing ties the layout's expectations to what the child supplied: a missing block renders as nothing, with no error and no test failure.
The shared state is a controller instance variable, so a partial rendered outside that controller reaches for a value that is not there.
